opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and honestly it's one of the things we think about the most. The way I'd frame it is: a really strong engineer who joins your team on day one is still not very productive, not because they lack skill, but because they lack context. They don't know where things live, what the conventions are, why that weird workaround exists in the build script. Models are in a similar position every time they start a task.

So a big part of making Codex effective is helping the model gather that context itself rather than expecting the user to hand-feed it everything. In the CLI, the model can actually explore the repo: it runs commands, greps around, reads files, looks at tests, tries things and sees what happens. That agentic loop of exploring and then acting turns out to be way more robust than trying to stuff the whole codebase into the prompt up front.

That said, there's some context that's really hard to infer just from reading code. Things like "we always run this particular lint command before committing," or "don't touch this directory, it's generated," or "here's how you run the test suite in this monorepo." For that, we lean on things like an AGENTS.md file, basically a README written for the agent, where teams can write down the tribal knowledge. And what we've seen is that the teams who invest a little bit in that, and in having good, fast tests the model can run to check its own work, get dramatically better results.

The last piece I'd mention is that the model being able to verify its work is itself a form of context. If it can run the tests, see the failure, and iterate, it learns a lot about the codebase in the process. So I think of it less as "how do we give the model all the context" and more as "how do we set up the environment so the model can go find the context it needs, the same way a good engineer would."

r001.rationale: The response says Codex can explore the repository to gather context, but does not state that models can do so rapidly.

r002.rationale: It describes an agentic loop of exploring and acting, but does not attribute effective tool use to reinforcement learning.

r003.rationale: It compares models to new engineers who lack context; it does not say models need to read less code than humans before building.

r004.rationale: It mentions AGENTS.md as repository guidance, but proposes no memory that persists between rollouts.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this is honestly one of the central questions. When we started building Codex CLI, the thing we kept coming back to is that the model is really only as good as the context it has access to, and in a real codebase the relevant context is almost never sitting in one place. It's spread across the files you're touching, the tests, the build system, the conventions the team has settled on over years, and a bunch of implicit knowledge that lives in people's heads.

So the way I think about it is in a few layers. The first layer is just the raw ability to look at the code. The model needs to be able to navigate, grep, read files, run things, and see the output. That sounds obvious, but a huge amount of the quality comes from the model being agentic about this, going and finding the context it needs rather than relying on whatever you happened to paste in. A good engineer who joins a new team doesn't ask you to describe the repo, they open it up and poke around, and we want the model to do the same thing.

The second layer is the stuff that isn't derivable from the code. Things like, we always run this linter before committing, or don't touch this directory because it's generated, or here's how we like to structure tests. That's where something like an AGENTS.md file comes in. It's basically a way for the team to write down the tribal knowledge once and have the model pick it up every time, instead of every engineer re-explaining it in every session.

And then the third layer, which I think is underappreciated, is the feedback loop. Context isn't just what you read before you start, it's what you learn as you go. If the model makes a change, runs the tests, and sees a failure, that failure is incredibly rich context. A lot of the capability jump we've seen comes from models getting better at using those signals, iterating against the real environment instead of guessing.

The thing we try hard to avoid is the idea that more context is always better. Dumping the entire repo into the window usually makes things worse, not better. What you want is the right context at the right moment, and the model being smart about going to get it. So a lot of our effort has been less about expanding the window and more about making the model a better investigator of the codebase it's working in.

r001.rationale: It says models should explore files and seek relevant context, but does not state that they can rapidly develop an understanding of the codebase.

r002.rationale: It describes learning from test failures and iterating, but does not attribute effective tool use to reinforcement learning.

r003.rationale: The human-engineer analogy is about exploring the repository; it does not say models need to read less code than humans before building.

r004.rationale: It describes AGENTS.md as recording team knowledge once for the model to pick up every session, communicating persistent context across sessions.

astra-6.text:
I think about it as giving the model enough context to make the same kinds of decisions an engineer would make. The immediate task is one piece of that, but there’s also the structure of the codebase, the conventions people follow, and how you validate that a change actually works.

With something like the Codex CLI, you don’t necessarily need to put all of that into the prompt upfront. The model can explore the repository, read relevant files, and build up context as it goes. The important thing is helping it find the right information and giving it a way to check its assumptions.

So I’d distinguish between context that’s discoverable in the code and context that lives in someone’s head. If there’s a particular reason you avoid a dependency, or a constraint that isn’t obvious from the implementation, making that explicit is really useful. Otherwise, you’re asking the model to infer something that even a new engineer on the team might not know.

r001.rationale: It says the model can explore the repository and read relevant files to build up context as it goes.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention reinforcement learning or explain tool use in terms of training toward outcomes.

r003.rationale: It says the model can discover context in the codebase, but does not compare how much code it needs to read with how much a human needs to read.

r004.rationale: It recommends making hidden constraints explicit, but does not propose persistent memory between rollouts.

sol-6.1.text:
I think about context as the information the model needs to close the loop on a task. Reading the code is part of that, but it also needs to understand what you’re trying to accomplish, what conventions the project follows, and how to tell whether a change actually works.

With the Codex CLI, you don’t necessarily have to put the entire codebase into the prompt. The model can explore: search for relevant files, follow dependencies, read the tests, and build up context as it goes. The important thing is giving it an environment where it can find that information and get useful feedback.

There’s also context that’s hard to infer from code—why a particular design decision was made, or a constraint that only exists in someone’s head. A little guidance there can go a long way. So I think it’s a combination of providing the intent and letting the agent discover the implementation details, then checking its work against tests and other signals.

r001.rationale: The response says the model can explore files and build context as it goes, but does not clearly state that it can develop this understanding rapidly.

r002.rationale: It does not attribute effective tool use to reinforcement learning or training to achieve outcomes.

r003.rationale: It says the model need not receive the entire codebase in its prompt, but does not say it needs to read less code than a human before building something.

r004.rationale: It does not propose memory that persists between rollouts.
